title: The binding in the morning
hook: many read the binding of Isaac each morning, asking for Abraham's devotion

segments.voice: Yesterday, the blessing over divrei Torah, with study right after it. Your line was learn something first. Today, one of the hardest stories in the Torah, read at the start of the day.

Genesis, chapter twenty-two. God tells Abraham to take his son Isaac up a mountain and offer him there. Abraham rises early, saddles the donkey, splits the wood. Father and son walk together for three days. On the mountain, Abraham builds an altar, binds his son, and lifts the knife. And an angel calls out and stops him. People have argued over this story for thousands of years; some of the most honest readers say it frightens them. And many Jews read it every morning, before breakfast.
screen: `GENESIS 22.` → `A FATHER, A SON, A KNIFE.` → `READ EVERY MORNING.`

segments.voice: In Hebrew it's the akedah, the binding, from the word for tying Isaac's hands and feet. The old Jewish translation opens the chapter: "God did prove Abraham." A test. When God calls, Abraham answers, "Here am I," and at the end, when the angel calls, he answers the same way. And the angel says: "Lay not thy hand upon the lad." Isaac isn't harmed. Why read it daily? The custom spread in the later Middle Ages, and the Shulchan Aruch, the sixteenth-century code of Jewish law, calls it good to say each morning. After it, many prayer books add a request, roughly: just as Abraham held back his compassion to do your will, so may your compassion hold back your anger from us. Abraham's devotion becomes something his children ask God to remember. The tradition calls this zechut avot, the merit of the ancestors: what the founders gave still counts for those who come after. Jews read this story many ways. Some see the height of faith: a person willing to give everything. Others stress the ending: the God of this story stops the knife, and many teachers have read it as a rejection of child sacrifice. Some live with the question and never settle it. Reading it every morning doesn't settle it either. It keeps the question, and the devotion, close.
screen: `AKEDAH: THE BINDING.` · `HERE AM I.` · `LAY NOT THY HAND UPON THE LAD.` · `ZECHUT AVOT: THE ANCESTORS' MERIT.` · then, large: `REMEMBER THE BINDING.`

segments.voice: Think of someone, in your family, your history, your neighborhood, who gave something costly for what they believed or loved: a grandparent who crossed an ocean, a parent who worked two jobs, a friend who kept a promise when it hurt. Picture one moment of that devotion, and ask quietly: what of theirs am I still living on? If you pray, you can ask God to remember them.
Akedah. The binding — Genesis twenty-two's story of Isaac bound on the altar, read daily by many Jews, asking God to remember Abraham's devotion.
Your line: remember the binding. The question stays open, and the devotion stays close. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Orthodox prayer books print the akedah (Genesis 22) near the start of the morning service with a request that follows it; some people say it privately each day, while other communities and prayer books leave it out.

chat.says: Why would anyone read the story of Abraham and Isaac every single morning?
options: Many then ask God to remember Abraham's devotion; the ancestors' goodness still counts for us.
Because reading it every day is how Jews finally settled what the story means.
Because the Talmud says it must be read first, before any other prayer is allowed.
